Christ teaches that one ought to deserve well of all, that even enemies should be loved, that one should freely lend, that vengeance should be taken against no one, and that one should give to every petitioner: on the contrary, the philosophers teach that this should be done only to those who compensate a benefit with a benefit; for the rest, it is permissible to be angry, to hate, to contend, to wage war, and to engage in usury. Furthermore, these men, with their free will and their dictates of right reason and the light of nature, have given us the <term>Pelagian</term> <gloss>a 5th-century Christian heresy denying original sin and asserting the capacity of human nature to achieve moral perfection</gloss> heretics. Moreover, the whole of moral philosophy (as <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus</note> Lactantius attests) is false and empty, neither instructing one in the duties of justice nor confirming the office and rational arguments of a human being. In short, it is entirely repugnant to the divine law and to Christ himself, such that its glory should be owed to no one other than Satan.

### ON POLITICS.
Chapter LV.

Politics also pertains to this philosophy, which is the art of administering the Republic. There are three species of it, namely: Monarchy, which is the rule of one; Aristocracy, which is the rule of the few, but of the noble,

<column-break/>

the wealthy, or the wise; and Democracy, which is the rule of the people. And related to all these are tyrannies, oligarchies, and anarchies. But all these things must be referred to that which comes to each person. For although the philosophers wish to define which is best, they follow diverse opinions: some, just as there is one God in heaven, one head in the members, and one leader among the bees, confess that Monarchy is the preferable form of correct government; thus others contend that Aristocracy, and others that Democracy, is the form of government that is equitable and by which liberty is preserved; above all others, however, are such as Plato, Aristotle, Apuleius, and others, who are not only from among our own, but also from among the barbarians. Those who have written about these matters do not speak except of those things that pertain to external administration, to peace, to the tranquility of public affairs, and to consultation, not to the soul, nor to salvation, nor to eternal aids: indeed, they look solely at those things which one might accomplish in this world. This is also what the legislators did, such as Lycurgus, Solon, and others, who <unclear>established</unclear> laws almost...

<summary>This passage contrasts the moral teachings of Christ with those of ancient philosophy, arguing that the latter is a false and potentially heretical vanity. It then introduces the study of politics as an art concerned only with worldly, temporal administration rather than eternal salvation.</summary>
